doc.title: James Hunter interviewed by Monk Rowe, Boston, Massachusetts, July 25, 2018

title: Song titles from familiar phrases
summary: Hunter explains how phrases such as 'This Is Where We Came In', 'Minute by Minute' and 'Let the Monkey Ride' became songs.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: If you get a phrase like that in your head do you — oh that could be a song?
Do you get the guitar and just start —

Sometimes yeah I’ll do that, and I’ll try and find things to do with it. A prime example is “This is Where We Came in” it’s a phrase that you don’t hear these days because cinemas don’t let people stay there for a second house do they. They chuck everybody out. And nowadays — you’d walk in halfway through a film and you’d sit it through to the end and wait for the adverts to come round and then catch up until the moment where, and that’s what, that’s that phrase people used to use. And I always thought that phrase was crying out to have a song made of it, like an analogy for a relationship that’s going tits up you know. You know, you can see where this is going you know. So that’s one I used. © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

And yeah, usually that’s the thing about pop music, it’s sort of a familiarity — if you sometimes write something that you’re surprised somebody hasn’t written already you know, that’s the kind of thing that somebody should have written by now. Why hasn’t somebody written a song called that. And that’s where I’m going. I think I’m starting from 1960 and sort of trying to point where, but for an accident of providence where popular music might have gone you know. But I’m developing it very slowly.
You’ve got a lot of ground to cover.
I suppose nowadays you could YouTube something and see if someone actually did write a song that — you’re thinking about a phrase and you mind find that —
Oh I’ve done that, I’ve done that with “Minute by Minute.” I saw that on a —

Yeah I didn’t know, I found out afterwards. I saw it on a picture of a film poster for a film called “Ring of Fire” with Dwayne Eddy doing the soundtrack and Frank Gorshin as the villain. It’s about a cop taking a hostage through a burning forest and the blurb on the thing says “Minute by minute” the something and it just stuck in my head and I went oh I’m having that. That just sounded good. And I checked, before I wrote it I checked to see if anyone had written one called that and Doobie Brothers had and I thought well sod it, I’m doing it anyway. Because you can’t copyright a phrase like that. I think a lot of my titles are fairly, you know, most of them would have been used in one shape or another before, except things like “Let the Monkey Ride.” That’s nobody’s.
I googled that phrase. I said to myself what does that mean.
It all came back to you. That’s all it was.
So I had to read the lyrics to figure it out for myself.

Yeah. That’s it. And it’s really, it was all used in the context of the well known phrase having a monkey on your back. That one I was going the opposite route of the Stones, you know, with “Brown Sugar.” You know they’re writing about you’re supposed to think they’re writing about a bird, you know, a girlfriend, and they’re actually writing about heroin. And I’m doing the opposite. I’m writing about the girl but trying to make it sound like it’s Persian rugs you know.
Yeah, yeah. That’s an ambiguous phrase as well.
